definition: An intent-to-use (ITU) application is a type of trademark application filed with the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) that allows an applicant to seek federal registration of a trademark before the mark is actually used in commerce. Under Section 1(b) of the Lanham Act, an ITU applicant must submit a verified declaration of bona fide intent to use the mark in commerce, which is made under oath and subject to criminal penalties for false statements. Filing an ITU application allows an applicant to secure a constructive use priority as of the application’s filing. This early priority can give the applicant an advantage over later filers in the event of a conflict at the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) or in litigation, even though the applicant has not yet begun using the mark. An ITU application does not mature into a registration until the applicant later proves actual use of the mark in commerce. After the application is approved, the USPTO issues a Notice of Allowance, and the applicant must file either:  A Statement of Use (SOU) showing use of the mark in commerce, or  A request for a six-month extension of time to file the SOU. Applicants may request up to five extensions (for a total of up to three years from the Notice of Allowance). If the applicant does not timely file a Statement of Use or extension request, the application will be abandoned. For more information on demonstrating bona fide intent, see Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure (TMEP) §1101. For timing requirements after a Notice of Allowance, see TMEP §§ 1108 – 1109.
